body:
Warren Buffett doesn’t drive a Lamborghini.
I learned that walking past a wall of Buffett’s investing rules I saw at a Jimmy John’s. I feel like it applies to a lot of what we covered last night on Predictable.
Last night was a primary night with almost no drama. Indiana races settled before polls closed. Vivek Ramaswamy was cruising most of the night with a near 99.3% chance to win Ohio’s gubernatorial primary.
On the surface, nothing to do.
That’s the trap.
The Bonding Trade
Here’s the move most people miss.
A market priced at 99% looks useless. 
What’s the point of a 1% gain?
Plenty, if it resolves tonight.
Your checking account earns 0.1%. A “high-yield” savings account earns maybe 4% a year. A 1% return in a single evening, on a near-certain outcome, isn’t a gimmick. It’s structural.
Stack a few of those a week. You’re outpacing every passive vehicle the average person has access to.
In prediction-market lingo, it’s called 
bonding
. Someone bought early, watched the contract climb to 99 cents, and wants their cash back. They sell at 99. You buy at 99. It resolves at a dollar. You take the penny.
It’s not glamorous. It’s not even clever. It’s just being willing to do something boring on a Tuesday while everyone else waits for an election they think is interesting.
Get the Most Conservative Person Who Can Win
The same discipline runs through politics.
Indiana’s primaries are loaded with revenge. Trump-endorsed challengers running against state senators who blocked his redistricting push.
I don’t love the redistricting fight, but let’s look at the game theory: once the redistricting wars start, like the Clone Wars once did, you really cannot stop pumping out clones.
The more durable insight is about candidate selection.
In a bright-red district, don’t run the loudest possible conservative. Run the most conservative 
electable
 person. Quality matters. Articulation matters. Ideology without competence is how Republicans lose Alabama Senate seats.
Same principle as the bonding trade. Don’t reach for the dramatic outcome. Find the maximum value at the highest probability of winning.
What the Markets Say About Iran
A Polymarket contract on a permanent U.S. and Iran peace deal:
4% by May 15
14% by end of May
37% by end of June
65% by year’s end
Every one of those is too high. A real, signed peace deal (not a vibes ceasefire) is closer to 5% by June and maybe 25% by year’s end.
Pair that with crude oil:
92% chance oil pierces $100 this month
60% chance it dips to $90
36% chance of a real spike to $120
Put the two markets together. The consensus is unmistakable.
The markets do not expect an oil crisis on our doorstep, and they do not expect nirvana either. They expect more of the same.
That’s the answer no one in cable news will give you. Nothing dramatic, in either direction, for a while.
Which is exactly the kind of forecast you can build a position around.
Hedge Your Life
One of the most useful frames 
Predictable
 offers.
My favorite example, which hopefully you’ll have memorized soon: the Philadelphia Eagles. As you know, I’m a big fan. If they win the Super Bowl, I’m elated and won’t care about whatever I lose taking an opposing position. I might lose, but at least I get paid for my misery.
The position doesn’t change the outcome. It does, however, change how a bad outcome feels.
The Iran market gives me the same emotional symmetry. Go “No” on a peace deal. If you lose, the war is over and you’re happy. If you win, you’re right and you get paid.
It’s a useful filter for any large, irreversible thing in your life. 
What outcome would ruin my week, and is there a market on it
“Yeah, We Will See What Happens”
Then there’s GameStop.
GameStop has made a $55.5 billion unsolicited bid for eBay. Half cash, half stock.
The math doesn’t quite work.
GameStop’s market cap is $11 billion. They have $9 billion in cash. Add a 
highly confident letter
 from TD for another $20 billion (not committed, just confident) and you’re at $40 billion.
You’re $16 billion short of the offer you’ve already made.
A reporter walks the CEO through this on air. The CEO’s answer: “Yeah, we will see what happens.”
That is not the answer of someone closing a $56 billion deal by December.
The market on whether GameStop acquires eBay this year was sitting at 22% when I looked at it. I ended up going No. 
Boring read, right read.
The Through-Line
Markets are mostly telling you what you already half-suspect.
Most of the time, the dramatic thing doesn’t happen. Most of the time, the boring base case wins.
Discipline is being willing to position yourself for that base case, even when it pays only a penny, because pennies, stacked correctly, beat almost everything else you could be doing.
You don’t have to find the dragon. You just have to not flinch when the market hands you 1%.
What to Do With This
Audit your idle cash.
 Could a portion of it be working in near-certain, short-duration positions instead of subsidizing your bank?
Look for the bonding trade.
 When a market sits at 95 to 99% on the day it resolves, ask whether the annualized yield beats what you’d otherwise earn.
Hunt secondary markets.
 Mispricings hide where attention isn’t. Don’t only fish in the headline contract.
Pick one outcome you can’t prevent but would hate.
 See if there’s a market that softens the emotional cost.
Treat “let us see what happens” as a tell.
 When a principal can’t walk you through their own math, that is information.
